sections.heading: Dialogue III, Knot iv, part 2 (printed pp. 296–306)
rows: Ereu. Nunc itaque dimittamus: & postquam consensum est aeterna neque finita, neque infinita esse posse, nisi aliquod unum saltem ex se existat, de eo conquiramus an intrinsecam aliquam radicem existendi habeat unde ab aeterno existentiam contrahat, an vero quasi casu contigerit hoc ens ab aeterno extitisse.

Ereu. Now therefore let us dismiss [it]: and since [postquam] it has been agreed that eternal [things] can be neither finite nor infinite unless some one [thing] at least exist from itself [ex se], concerning it let us search out [conquiramus] whether it has some intrinsic root [radicem] of existing, whence it draws [contrahat] existence from eternity, or truly whether as if by chance [casu] it happened that this being [ens] existed from eternity.
Asphal. Usque adeone insaniuisse quemquam existimas ut ens quod a se sit, non existimauerit radicem existendi in sese habere, ut hoc saxum mouere velis?

Asphal. Do you think anyone to have gone mad so far [Usque adeone] that he did not think a being which is from itself [a se] to have the root of existing in itself, that you wish to move this stone [saxum movere]?

Ereu. Immo vero & Philosophorum proceres: ut enim taceam Democritum & Epicurum (quorum tamen ille inter sapientissimos collocatur) quid Platoni dices & iis qui aërem, aquam vel terram aeterna posuerunt & menti vel Deo coaeua? num putes negauisse similia interire posse, quae tamen a se & non a Deo existere censuerunt, Deoque tantum immutandi potestatem concesserunt. Immo quoties in illud eorum axioma, ex nihilo nihil, respicio, vereor ne omnes antiquos idem inuoluerit error: quare nisi aliud praeoptas hoc agamus. Et in primis non tam peto quam praesumo eandem (quae rei praesenti est ad existendum necessitas) etiam praeteritis, pro sua duratione non inextitisse modo; sed immutatam in esse; quandoquidem quae facta sunt, infecta fieri, omnem potentiam excedere in confesso sit.

Ereu. Nay rather [Immo vero] even the chiefs [proceres] of the Philosophers: for, that I may be silent about Democritus and Epicurus (of whom nevertheless the former [ille] is placed among the wisest), what will you say to Plato and to those who posited air, water or earth [as] eternal and coeval with Mind or God? would you think [that they] denied that like [things] [similia] can perish, which nevertheless they judged [censuerunt] to exist from themselves and not from God, and to God they conceded only the power [potestatem] of changing [immutandi]? Nay, as often as I look back [respicio] to that axiom of theirs, ‘from nothing nothing’, I fear lest the same error has enveloped all the ancients: wherefore, unless you prefer something else, let us do this [hoc agamus]. And in the first place I do not so much ask as presume that the same (the necessity which a present thing has to existing [quae rei praesenti est ad existendum necessitas]) not only has existed-in [inextitisse] past things too, for their duration, but is in [them] [in esse] unchanged; since [quandoquidem] that things which have been done [facta] should become undone [infecta fieri] exceeds every power [potentiam] is confessed [in confesso sit].
Andab. De hoc nemo contenderit, fuisse enim & non fuisse aeque pugnant, atque non esse cum esse.
Andab. About this no one would contend, for to have been and not to have been fight [pugnant] equally as not to be with to be.

Ereu. Neque hoc negabis mihi gratiae ut saecula anteriora & ulteriora quibusuis positis pro libito fingam, modo ne finem excedam. Hoc enim omni quantitati commune est priuilegium, ut mente semper ampliari valeat.

Ereu. Nor will you deny me this by way of favour [gratiae], that I may feign [fingam] at pleasure [pro libito] ages [saecula] anterior and further [ulteriora] than any [ages] posited, provided I do not exceed the end. For this is a privilege common to every quantity, that it can always be enlarged [ampliari] by the mind.
Andab. Sic est.
Andab. So it is.
Ereu. Num & hoc: quod in quolibet horum signo verum est, hoc uniuersaliter verum esse, id est semper verum.
Ereu. [Will you deny] this too: that what is true in any sign [signo] whatever of these, this is universally true, that is, always true?
Andab. Hic haereo.
Andab. Here I stick [haereo].
Ereu. Cur haeres? Cum singula eadem sint & omnia: & omnia quae tempus omne, seu semper: si enim non semper id verum sit, imaginabile erit signum in quo non sit verum.

Ereu. Why do you stick? Since ‘the singulars’ [singula] and ‘all’ are the same: and ‘all’ [the same] as ‘all time’, or ‘always’: for if that be not always true, there will be an imaginable sign in which it is not true.
Andab. Persuasisti.
Andab. You have persuaded [me].

Ereu. Nunc itaque attende num aliquid efficiatur necne? Ens quod non habet necessitatem in se existendi, potest non existere. Fingantur itaque sursum versus tempora quotlibet & quantalibet, nullum erit signum in quo non sit verum hoc Ens posse non existere. Rursus nullum est signum in iisdem saeculis, ante quod saecula sine fine non sint ficticia, unde rursus in quolibet signo omnium saeculorum fictorum, verum erit non posse non extitisse per infinita saecula. Vide an haec non eam vim habeant. Ens illud semper potuit non esse & ens illud semper non potuit non esse, seu quod idem est, nunquam potuit non esse.

Ereu. Now therefore attend whether something is effected [efficiatur] or not. A Being which has not the necessity in itself of existing [necessitatem in se existendi] can not-exist. Let there be feigned therefore upward [sursum versus] times as many as you please and as great as you please [quotlibet & quantalibet]: there will be no sign in which this is not true, ‘the Being can not-exist’. Again, there is no sign in the same ages before which ages without end are not feignable [ficticia]; whence again in any sign whatever of all the feigned ages it will be true [that it] cannot not-have-existed through infinite ages. See whether these [things] have not this force: ‘That being always could not-be’, and ‘that being always could not not-be’, or, what is the same, ‘never could not-be’.

Andab. Mihi neutiquam haec eorum intellectio allucet, video enim alteram propositionem de praeterito esse, alteram de praesenti, unde cum de diuersis sint quomodo ullam oppositionem implicent, non capio.

Andab. To me this understanding [intellectio] of them by no means shines [allucet]; for I see the one proposition to be about the past, the other about the present; whence, since they are about diverse [things], how they involve [implicent] any opposition, I do not grasp.

Ereu. Anxie obuiasti. Oportet itidem scrupulose me incedere. Ais te videre alteram propositionem de praeterito esse, alteram de praesenti. Sed attende ne sis deceptus. Hae enim propositiones, in hoc signo A, potest non esse, & in hoc signo A, non potest non fuisse, sunt altera de praesenti, altera de praeterito. Verum has intuere, in quolibet signo A, potest non esse, & in quolibet signo A, non potest non fuisse; & quoniam τὸ in quolibet signo, uniuersale est, & subiectum uniuersalitatis est tempus; omne autem tempus differentias praeteriti & praesentis excludit, siue malis, includit, fit respectu harum propositionum, nihil praeteritum vel praesens (prout contra se inuicem distinguuntur) esse posse, etiamsi utrumque a propositione comprehendatur. Quod apparebit si vice τοῦ in quolibet signo subieceris semper. Dicamus itaque semper potest non esse, nonne vides nihil esse reliqui, in quo non possit non esse, & rursus semper non potuit non fuisse: non palam est respectu τοῦ semper, nihil praeteritum esse posse. Et hanc proinde propositionem vel falsam esse, vel necessarium esse ut in aliquo praesenti non possit non esse, quod reliqua contradicit.

Ereu. You have met [me] anxiously [Anxie obviasti]. I must likewise proceed scrupulously. You say you see the one proposition to be about the past, the other about the present. But attend lest you be deceived. For these propositions, ‘in this sign A it can not-be’ and ‘in this sign A it cannot not-have-been’, are the one about the present, the other about the past. But look at [intuere] these: ‘in any sign A whatever it can not-be’ and ‘in any sign A whatever it cannot not-have-been’; and since the ‘in any sign whatever’ [τὸ in quolibet signo] is universal, and the subject of the universality is time; and all time excludes the differences of past and present, or, if you prefer [sive malis], includes [them]; it comes about [fit] with respect to these propositions that nothing can be past or present (according as they are distinguished against one another), even if each is comprehended by the proposition. Which will appear if in place of the ‘in any sign whatever’ you subjoin [subieceris] ‘always’. Let us say therefore ‘always it can not-be’: do you not see that nothing is left over in which it may not be able not-to-be [non possit non esse]; and again ‘always it could not not-have-been’: is it not open [palam] that with respect to the ‘always’ nothing can be past? And therefore that this proposition is either false, or it is necessary that in some present it cannot not-be, which contradicts the rest.
Andab. Non possum inficias ire quin τὸ semper nihil esse praeteritum valeat: sed non tantumdem video in τῷ in quolibet signo. Ante quodlibet enim aliud signum reperiri potest.

Andab. I cannot go into denial [inficias ire] that the ‘always’ avails [valeat] [to make] nothing to be past: but I do not see as much [tantumdem] in the ‘in any sign whatever’. For before any whatever another sign can be found.

Ereu. Duo videntur esse quae intuitum tuum distringunt, alterum est quod apparet tibi τὸ in quolibet signo, particularis esse propositio & non uniuersalis: Ceu non tantum valere, quam si in unoquoque vel omni signo diceretur. Quod autem te fortius illigat est quod rationem infiniti realem & possibilem semper imaginaris, neque expectas contradictionem in eo inuenire: & ideo refugis eadem credere in quolibet signo & semper: quia ante quodlibet signum ex ratione infiniti necessum est infinita priora reperiri.

Ereu. Two [things] seem to be which distract [distringunt] your gaze [intuitum]: the one is that the ‘in any sign whatever’ appears to you to be a particular proposition and not a universal: as though [Ceu] [it did] not avail as much as if it were said ‘in each one’ or ‘in every sign’. But what binds you more strongly [fortius illigat] is that you always imagine the notion [rationem] of the infinite [as] real and possible, nor do you expect to find contradiction in it: and therefore you shrink [refugis] from believing the same [things] in ‘any sign whatever’ and ‘always’: because before any sign whatever, from the notion [ratione] of the infinite, it is necessary [necessum est] that infinite prior [signs] be found.

Andab. Caue ne te deficiat memoria: quomodo enim explicas nobis per infinitum rationem existendi ab aeterno, si infiniti ratio implicatoria est. Adiecta enim ratione quae opposita implicat in se, facile erit ipsa opposita nobis offerre, non quae in re sint, sed quae in eo quod abs ipso te adiectum est, reperiantur.

Andab. Beware lest memory fail you: for how do you explain to us through the infinite the reason [rationem] of existing from eternity, if the notion [ratio] of the infinite is implicatory [implicatoria]? For a notion [ratione] having been added which implies opposites in itself, it will be easy to offer us the opposites themselves, not [such] as are in the thing [in re], but [such] as are found in that which has been added by you yourself.
Ereu. Sed non ego ratione infiniti usus sum, verum ea temporum precaria fictione, sine qua durationem non intelligimus, & in qua nihil contradictionis est, nisi adiiciamus unde implicetur.

Ereu. But I did not use the notion [ratione] of the infinite, but that precarious [precaria] fiction of times, without which we do not understand duration, and in which there is nothing of contradiction, unless we add [something] whence it may be implicated [implicetur].
Andab. In ea fictione qua tu usus es, verum est ante quodlibet signum alia esse infinita, siue malis, in infinitum.
Andab. In that fiction which you used, it is true that before any sign whatever others are infinite, or, if you prefer, to infinity.

Ereu. Recte. Palam itaque est dum de iis quae in potentia sunt, loquimur (sicut cum quantitatem mente extendimus) nullam esse contradictionem hanc autem ex subiecto contingere quod ponimus actu fuisse. Hinc itaque oppositio quod ex adiecta subiecti existentia saecula quasi coexistentiam assumunt.

Ereu. Rightly. It is open therefore that while we speak of those [things] which are in potency (as when we extend quantity by the mind) there is no contradiction, but that this [contradiction] befalls [contingere] from the subject which we posit to have been in act. Hence therefore [comes] the opposition: that from the added existence of the subject the ages take on as it were [quasi] coexistence.
Andab. Subtile admodum est quod expressisti; accrescit tamen mihi quo magis meditor, euidentia; vere enim impossibile est ut semper possit non esse & semper non potuerit non esse.
Andab. Very subtle is what you have expressed; yet the more I meditate, [the more] evidence [evidentia] grows for me; for truly it is impossible that it always can not-be and always could not not-be.
[Margin, p. 301: Nullum corpus ab aeterno fuisse.]
[Margin, p. 301: That no body has been from eternity.]

Ereu. Et quid de hoc existimas? potuisse non fuisse, & in nullo signo potuisse non fuisse? sed adiice necessitatem existendi ei quod est (hoc est) repugnantiam ad non essendum esse: ergo vel per extrinsecum (sicut quae causantur) repugnabit vel per extrinseca, sed in confesso est non per extrinsecum repugnare τῷ non esse, intrinsecam itaque habet repugnantiam: Demonstratum itaque habes corpus nullum ab aeterno extitisse, postquam ex hesterna digladiatione, certum est corpori omni interire posse naturale esse. Neque interfit (quantum ego video) an a causa, an a se esse habeat, modo tale sit, ut cum posse non esse consistat: Ex his enim pure terminis, ab aeterno extitit & potuit non esse, connexa est tota argumenti series.

Ereu. And what do you think about this: to have been able not-to-have-been, and in no sign to have been able not-to-have-been? But add that the necessity of existing to that which is, is (that is [hoc est]) repugnance to not-being [ad non essendum]: therefore it will be repugnant either through [something] extrinsic (as [are] the things which are caused) or through extrinsic [things] [per extrinseca; sic, read intrinseca?]; but it is confessed that it is not repugnant to the not-being [τῷ non esse] through [something] extrinsic; therefore it has an intrinsic repugnance. You have it demonstrated therefore that no body has existed from eternity, since [postquam] from yesterday’s sword-fight [digladiatione] it is certain that to be able to perish is natural to every body. Nor does it matter [interfit] (so far as I see) whether it has being [esse] from a cause or from itself, provided it be such that it is consistent with being able not-to-be: for from these terms purely, ‘existed from eternity’ and ‘could not-be’, the whole series of the argument is connected.

Asphal. Videtur adhuc mihi in vocibus aliqua subesse ambiguitas, quae demonstrationem, nisi inuigiles, supplantare possit. Alia enim potentia est intrinseca & naturalis, ut ipsemet declarasti, cum de infinito ageres, alia extrinseca & Logicalis. Quid itaque vetat potentiam naturalem ad non esse cum ea quae ex omnium circumstantium consideratione dicitur, impotentia consistere; ex eo quod alio & alio sensu nomen potentiae usurpatur.

Asphal. There seems to me still some ambiguity to underlie [subesse] in the words [vocibus], which, unless you keep watch [invigiles], may trip up [supplantare] the demonstration. For one potency [potentia] is intrinsic and natural, as you yourself declared when you were treating of the infinite, another extrinsic and Logical. What therefore forbids natural potency to not-being to consist with that impotency which is spoken of from the consideration of all the circumstances [circumstantium]; from this, that the name of potency is used [usurpatur] in one and another sense?

Ereu. Immo utraque pars impotentiam & potentiam extrinsecam accipit: harum enim propositionum utramque necessum est esse veram de potentia extrinseca. Non potuit non fuisse in infinitis instantibus & nullum signare potest instans in quo non potuerit non fuisse accipiendo in utraque propositione possibilitatem extrinsecam. Praeterea hoc vide: impotentiam extrinsecam cum potentia extrinseca incompossibilem esse, in concessis est. Sublatam itaque hanc impotentiam necessum est. Vel itaque per successionem quam supra concessisti non posse huic malo mederi, vel per effectum permanentem. Fit itaque datam esse creaturae simultaneam aliquam ad non esse per infinita tempora in indiuisibili operantem repugnantiam, id est, huic essentiae repugnare aliquando non fuisse. Hanc considera an cum potentia naturali ad non essendum conciliare valeas. Verum neque Syllogismum quo prius Celsi Paralogismum fuisse concesserim, sed responsionem tuam corpore (ut aiunt) vitaui ne in abstractam nimium & perplexam vos contemplationem traherem.

Ereu. Nay, each part takes impotency and potency [as] extrinsic: for it is necessary that each of these propositions be true of extrinsic potency: ‘It was not able not-to-have-been in infinite instants’ and ‘[one] can mark [signare] no instant in which it was not able not-to-have-been’, taking [accipiendo] in each proposition extrinsic possibility. Besides, see this: that extrinsic impotency is incompossible with extrinsic potency is among the things conceded [in concessis est]. It is necessary therefore [that] this impotency [be] taken away [Sublatam]. Either therefore by succession, which above you conceded cannot remedy this evil, or by a permanent effect. It comes about [Fit] therefore that there has been given to the creature some simultaneous repugnance to not-being, operating through infinite times in an indivisible [in indivisibili]; that is, [that] to this essence it is repugnant at some time not to have been. Consider this, whether you can reconcile [it] with natural potency to not-being. But neither would I have conceded the Syllogism by which earlier [prius] [I argued] to have been a Paralogism of Celsus [Celsi]; but I avoided your answer with the body [corpore] (as they say), lest I should draw you into a contemplation too abstract and perplexed.

Andab. Quid ais, Asphali, putasne ferendam hanc iniuriam, qua nos affecit Ereunius, ut speciem ostentaret nescio quam, & iam inescatos & nihil cogitantes ipse praemeditatus oppresserit, coëgeritque fateri aliud longe diuersum quam quod sperabamus?

Andab. What do you say, Asphalius, do you think this injury [iniuriam] to be borne, with which Ereunius has affected us, so that he might show off [ostentaret] some appearance [speciem] or other [nescio quam], and [that] he himself, premeditated, has overwhelmed [us] already baited [inescatos] and thinking of nothing, and has compelled [us] to confess another [thing] far different from what we were hoping?

Asphal. Ego vero censeo dolo malo actum, & suo damno fecisse, & si tuum calculum meo addideris, damnandum esse, ut quam ostentauit spem conditoris mundi nobis, demonstrandi, ratam faxit, & rem ipsam praestet.

Asphal. I for my part judge [censeo] [that] it has been acted with evil fraud [dolo malo], and [that he] has done [it] to his own loss [suo damno], and, if you add your vote [calculum] to mine, [that he] is to be condemned, so that the hope which he showed off to us, of demonstrating the founder [conditoris] of the world, he make ratified [ratam faxit], and perform [praestet] the thing itself.

Ereu. Heu me! quibus incidi tortoribus! quibus quo magis satisfeceris, magis famelicos reddideris. Saturate vos hac vice, si enim effugero manus vestras, non amplius me illaqueabitis. Habetis iam conclusum esse aliquod Ens a se quod non possit non esse. Putatisne hanc necessitatem effectiuam esse vel formalem?

Ereu. Ah me! upon what torturers have I fallen! whom the more you shall have satisfied, the more famished you shall have rendered [them]. Sate yourselves this time [hac vice]; for if I escape your hands, you will not ensnare me any more. You have it now concluded that there is some Being from itself [Ens a se] which cannot not-be. Do you think this necessity to be effective [effectivam] or formal?
[Margin, p. 304: Existentiam enti a se essentialem esse.]
[Margin, p. 304: That existence is essential to a being from itself.]
Andab. Cum existentiam ab alio non accipiat, neque res ipsa possit ad se efficiendum concurrere: in propatulo est formalem esse non effectiuam hanc necessitatem.
Andab. Since it does not receive existence from another, nor can the thing itself concur to effecting itself: it is in the open [in propatulo] that this necessity is formal, not effective.
Ereu. Si formalis sit, vel identicam seu potius identitatem esse palam est, vel unitatem aliquam minorem: utram das?
Ereu. If it be formal, it is open that it is either identical [identicam], or rather identity, or some lesser unity: which do you give?

Andab. Identitati faueo, sed nescio an conuincendae sint. Formalis enim cum sit necessitas ex terminis esse videtur, terminorum vero unitas identitas est: videmus enim praedicatione, seu affirmatione quod unum sit alterum, eam explicari.

Andab. I favour identity, but I do not know whether they are to be proven [convincendae sint]. For since it is formal, the necessity seems to be from the terms, but the unity of terms is identity: for we see it [eam] to be explained by predication, or affirmation, that one is the other.

Ereu. Sed ea quae praedicantur videmus contingere ut accidentalia sint, & communi aliquo conueniant. Unde modo τὸ existens commune sit, existentiam eandem esse existenti, non fit necessarium. Vide itaque an inde confici aliquid possit, quod quo minor est unitas eo maior sit diuisibilitas, postquam unum esse, est esse indiuisum. Quoniam itaque nulla realis est diuisibilitas inter existentiam & ens a se, iam enim consensum est illud non posse non esse, fit omnino indiuisibilitatem, seu simplicitatem, seu identitatem realem apud ea inueniri.

Ereu. But the things which are predicated we see happen [contingere] to be accidental, and to agree in something common. Whence, provided the ‘existent’ [τὸ existens] be common, it does not become [fit] necessary that existence is the same as the existent. See therefore whether from this something can be accomplished [confici]: that the less is the unity, the greater is the divisibility, since [postquam] to be one is to be undivided. Since therefore there is no real divisibility between existence and the being from itself [ens a se], for it has already been agreed that that cannot not-be, it comes about that altogether indivisibility, or simplicity, or real identity is found with them [apud ea].
Andab. Euicisti.
Andab. You have carried it [Evicisti].
Ereu. Nunc hoc attendamus an essentialis aeterno Enti sit existentia quam eandem esse confessus es. Quid censes?
Ereu. Now let us attend to this: whether existence, which you have confessed to be the same, is essential to the eternal Being. What do you judge?

Andab. Essentiam ab essendo dictam video & ens quasi participium τοῦ esse. Essentia itaque non potest esse aliud quam τὸ quo res est seu existit; ita ut si plura in re aliqua sint habentia ordinem, respectu existentiae, & aliud plus, aliud minus conferat ad existentiam seu connectatur cum ea, palam fit quae magis conferunt, & quae magis connectuntur, magis essentialium rationem habere, quam quae minus. Et haec quidem vera sunt in iis quae ex sese potentialiter tantum existunt, & ab alio accipiunt actu existere. Si modo haec transferamus ad entia, quorum entitas sit eorum existentia, clarum est, quod in eorum entitate maxime confert ad existentiam & connectitur cum ea, esse ipsam rationem existentiae: hanc itaque maxime essentialem & caeteris formaliorem talis entis seu partem, seu differentiam, seu notionem ego iudicarem. Et si qui contentiose vellent disputare, ea tantummodo pertinere ad essentiam quae existentiae contra diuiduntur, puto eos de nomine litigatum ire, & negare non posse esse in hoc ente aliquid formalius, quod quo nomine velint appellari ipsi videant: mihi certum est praecipuum & principale in ipsa re esse, cum caetera quaecumque sint in rebus quasi gradus quidam & dispositiones ad existentiam sint.

Andab. I see essence [Essentiam] [to be] named [dictam] from being [ab essendo], and a being [ens] [to be] as it were the participle of the ‘to be’ [τοῦ esse]. Essence therefore cannot be other than the ‘that by which’ [τὸ quo] a thing is or exists; so that if there be several [things] in some thing having order with respect to existence, and one contributes [conferat] more, another less to existence, or is connected with it, it becomes open that those which contribute more, and which are more connected, have more the nature [rationem] of essentials than those which [do so] less. And these [things] indeed are true in those which of themselves exist only potentially, and receive from another to exist in act. If now [Si modo] we transfer these [things] to beings whose entity [entitas] is their existence, it is clear that what in their entity most contributes to existence and is connected with it, is the very notion [rationem] of existence: this therefore I would judge [to be] the most essential and more formal than the rest, whether part, or difference [differentiam], or notion of such a being. And if any would wish contentiously to dispute that those [things] only pertain to essence which are divided against [contra dividuntur] existence, I think they are going to litigate [litigatum ire] about a name, and [that they] cannot deny that there is in this being something more formal; by what name they wish it to be called, let them see for themselves: to me it is certain that [it] is the chief [praecipuum] and principal [thing] in the thing itself, since the rest, whatever be in things, are as it were certain grades [gradus] and dispositions to existence.

Ereu. Mihi satisfecisti, alij videant quomodo ipsis arrideant quae dixisti. Sed quid est quod sub ipso exitu orationis tuae dixisti, caetera omnia quasi dispositiones quasdam & gradus esse ad existentiam? si enim hoc verum est, nihil essentiale existentiae potest aduenire.

Ereu. You have satisfied me; let others see how the things which you have said smile upon [arrideant] them. But what is it which under the very exit [exitu] of your speech you said, that all the rest are as it were certain dispositions and grades to existence? for if this is true, nothing essential can come to [advenire] existence.
Andab. Nihil certius.
Andab. Nothing more certain.
[Here (p. 306, margin ‘Nodus V. Ens a se unicum esse & caeterorum causam’) Knot v begins with Ereunius’ ‘Ergo si poneretur existentiae subsistentis…’.]
[Here (p. 306, margin ‘Knot V. That the being from itself is unique and the cause of the rest’) Knot v begins with Ereunius’ ‘Therefore if there were posited…’.]

terms: labour in vain; stir up an obvious matter; also ‘move a stone that should lie’ (proverb: ‘ne moveas saxum’).
Proverbial (cf. Sisyphus; Erasmus, Adagia ‘saxum volvere’): Asphalius thinks it absurd to argue that a self-existent being has its root of existing in itself.
the axiom ‘nothing comes from nothing’ (Lucretius I.150, Parmenides, Aristotle Phys. I.4).
White blames this axiom for the ancients’ belief that matter or elements are self-existent and uncreated.
not only to have existed-in … but to be in
inexsisto ‘exist in, be present in’ (+ dative praeteritis); ‘in esse’ probably = inesse ‘be in’; alternatively ‘in being’ (in esse).
The claim that past existence is necessary (quod factum est infectum fieri nequit: cf. Aristotle EN VI.2, Agathon) is the premise of the whole argument against an eternal contingent being.
the classical topos ‘factum infectum fieri non potest’ (Plautus, Aul. 741; Aristotle EN 1139b).
Even divine power does not extend to making the past not to have been (Aquinas ST I.25.4).
instant, point of time; ‘in quolibet signo’ = at any instant.
Scholastic ‘signum’ (as in ‘signa rationis’, ‘in signo priori’); kept as ‘sign’ per glossary.
Greek article substantivising a word or proposition (‘the in-any-sign-whatever’).
School usage; case of the article follows the construction.
imagined, supposed; ‘precarious’ = granted by request, on sufferance (precarium), not real.
White’s ‘imaginary time’: the mind can always feign earlier ages, but this is a fiction asked for, not a real infinite.
Scholastic: a notion that ‘implicat’ is self-contradictory.
potentia / impotentia intrinseca, naturalis vs extrinseca, Logicalis
potency / impotency, intrinsic, natural vs extrinsic, Logical
physical/real potency vs logical possibility judged ‘ex omnium circumstantium consideratione’.
Scholastic distinction between potentia physica and potentia logica (non-repugnance of terms); White argues both sides of the contradiction use extrinsic potency.
at a single indivisible instant; non-successively.
Refers back to the previous day’s discussion (Dialogue II) of the corruptibility of bodies; gladiatorial metaphor for disputation.
Celsus the anti-Christian philosopher (Origen, Contra Celsum); or the jurist Juventius Celsus, whose curt ‘responsio Celsina’ (Dig. 28.1.27) was proverbial; possibly a misprint.
avoid with the body (as they say)
Continues the sword-fight metaphor: Ereunius sidestepped Andabata’s objection instead of parrying it.
dolo malo / suo damno / calculus / ratam facere / praestare
with evil fraud / to his own loss / vote / make ratified / perform
Roman-law and court vocabulary: dolus malus (fraud), calculus (pebble = vote), ratum facere (ratify), praestare (make good).
Mock-trial conceit, as in D3-N02 part 2; ‘faxit’ is the archaic legal subjunctive.
necessity from an efficient cause vs from the form/essence itself.
Scholastic: the self-existent’s necessity is not caused but formal, from its essence.
real identity vs lesser (formal, modal) unity.
Scotist/Thomist debates on distinction of essence and existence; White argues for real identity in the ens a se.
essentia ab essendo; ens quasi participium τοῦ esse
essence named from being; a being as it were the participle of ‘to be’
Thomist commonplace (De ente et essentia); ens as participle of esse.
the formal principle by which a thing is (quo est vs quod est).
Boethian/scholastic quo est / quod est distinction.
White makes existence the most formal element and everything else a disposition toward it; this sets up Knot v.

Knot v begins on p. 306 (PDF 317) with Ereunius’ ‘Ergo si poneretur existentiae subsistentis…’ (margin ‘Nodus V. Ens a se unicum esse & caeterorum causam’). Offset +11 holds. Signatures: Pp (p. 297), Pp ij (p. 299), Pp iij (p. 301), Qq (p. 305).

Uncertain readings and constructions: (1) p. 297 ‘non inextitisse modo; sed immutatam in esse’ — taken as inexsisto ‘exist in’ + dative and ‘in esse’ = inesse; ‘non … modo’ = ‘not only’. (2) p. 297 ‘negabis mihi gratiae’ — genitive of manner (‘by way of favour’) or dative; sense the same. (3) p. 298 ‘seu quod idem, est nunquam potuit non esse’ — printed comma before ‘est’; repunctuated ‘quod idem est,’. (4) p. 299 ‘nihil esse reliqui, in quo non possit non esse’ — rendered literally; the sense is that no time remains in which it lacks the potency to not-be. (5) p. 301 ‘vel per extrinseca’ — the second alternative should logically be ‘intrinseca’ (as the conclusion ‘intrinsecam itaque habet repugnantiam’ shows); probably a misprint; translated as printed with a note. (6) p. 302 ‘circumstantium’ printed for ‘circumstantiarum’ (or ‘of all the bystanders/surrounding things’). (7) p. 303 ‘neque Syllogismum quo prius Celsi Paralogismum fuisse concesserim’ — reading of ‘Celsi’ is clear on the image, but the allusion is uncertain (Celsus the anti-Christian polemicist? the jurist Celsus? a misprint?); the construction is elliptical; rendered literally with supplied ‘[I argued]’. (8) p. 304 ‘nescio an conuincendae sint’ — feminine plural subject unclear (perhaps the two alternatives, identity and lesser unity, or ‘the terms’ loosely); rendered ‘whether they are to be proven’. (9) p. 304 ‘affirmatione’ partly obscured by an ink blot; reading certain from context. No illegible readings.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images and the English after drafting. The separate check produced 2 corrections: (i) p. 298 ‘necessitatem in se existendi’ re-ordered to follow the Latin (‘the necessity in itself of existing’), since ‘in se’ may go with ‘necessitatem’ rather than ‘existendi’; (ii) p. 303 ‘quo magis satisfeceris, magis … reddideris’ — future perfects restored (‘shall have satisfied … shall have rendered’). Revisions already made while drafting: (a) p. 297 the parenthesis ‘(quae rei praesenti est ad existendum necessitas)’ first rendered as a separate clause, re-attached as apposition to ‘eandem’; (b) p. 298 ‘ficticia’ first rendered ‘fictitious’, changed to ‘feignable’ to keep the potential sense (‘are not [able to be] feigned’); (c) p. 301 ‘adiice necessitatem … repugnantiam … esse’ restructured as indirect statement (‘add that the necessity … is repugnance’); (d) p. 302 ‘non potuit non fuisse’ / ‘non potuerit non fuisse’ harmonised as ‘was not able not-to-have-been’; (e) p. 303 ‘Fit … datam esse’ — ‘has been given’ (perfect infinitive) restored, earlier draft had ‘is given’.
